full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by leave by the appellants is directed against the judgment and order dated August 23, 2003 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.71 of 2001 arising out of the judgment and decree dated 8-1-2001 passed by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Third Court (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka in Title Suit No.153 of 2000 dismissing the same upon setting aside the award dated 5-2-2000 passed by the sole arbitrator. 

 9. Mr Rajik-al-Jalil, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the contractor is entitled to compensation for breach of contract and that in the case in hand, the High Court Division without at all taking into consideration section 73 of the Contract Act awarded the full amount of the contract value although admittedly no work was done under the contract other than collecting some construction materials at the site. He further submits that the award being otherwise invalided for non-performance of contract, the High Court Division erred in law awarding Taka 92, 55,140 in respect of arrear of contract money causing failure of justice thereby. He also submits that though the appellants failed to deposit the amount which, they were required to pay under the award or furnished security to the satisfaction of the Court for payment of such sum or for fulfillment of any other obligation by them under the award, it would be open to the Court to consider the patent defect in the award suo motu and when the Court acts suo motu, no question of limitation can arise and no action regarding making of deposit can also arise and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. 

 10. Mr Ahsanul Karim, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondent, on the other hand, submits that the application in the form of written objection laid under section 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 was no application nor written objection and the same was not entertain able as the appellants did not deposit the amount which they were required to pay under the award to furnish security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum, and that the High Court Division has given elaborate finding with reference to many leading cases and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the High Court Division came to a finding that the appellants could not make out a case of misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator and, as such, the question of interference with the impugned judgment does not arise at all. He also submits that regarding setting aside of the award relating to Taka 92,55,140 no objection was raised by the appellants and, as such, no interference is called for. He lastly submits that the Court can-not see the correctness of the award and that the modified award passed by the High Court Division should be maintained. 

 "Admittedly no work being done under the contract other than collecting some construction material at the site, the High Court Division acted without jurisdiction in awarding almost the full amount of contract value as "arrears of contract money" and interest on the said amount as compensatory cost without any basis whatsoever either in law or on facts. The award being otherwise invalid for non-performance of the contract work, High Court Division grievously erred in awarding Taka 92,55,140 as "in respect of arrears of contract money" causing grave failure of justice thereby. The High Court Division erred in holding that "by not raising any objection to jurisdiction of Arbitrator to deal with Arbitration matter partly waived his right in putting forward any objection to jurisdiction of Arbitrator to arbitrate the dispute 'and pass award after the award. The High Court Division erred in holding that the learned Subordinate Judge "Virtually sat on appeal. The High Court Division erred in holding "the decision raised by court on "Misconduct' suffers from patent illegality" by theorizing about misconduct on irrelevant basis. The award being made without jurisdiction, High Court Division erred in holding "we are of this mediated view that the application in the form of written objections laid under section 33 of the Arbitration Act was' no application nor written objection and the same was not at all entertain able. In cases of award without jurisdiction or preposterous award having no nexus with the contract, whether deposes: in court is sine qua non for having the effect of the award determined, being a question of great Public importance needs to be authoritatively settled by this Hon'ble Court". 

 13. At the outset, Mr Ahsanul Karim submits that he will not press Civil Appeal No.75 of 2006 filed against the judgment of the High Court Division so far as it relates to the part of award not granting damage for loss of goodwill and reputation of business amounting to Taka 6 (six) crore. The High Court Division gave elaborate finding on section 33 of the Arbitration Act, on misconduct on the part of the arbitrator and on the validity of appointment of Mr Asaduzzaman as the sole Arbitrator. 

 17. When an employer commits breach of contract, the contractor is entitled to claim damages. But what will be the measure of damages? Section 73 of the Contract Act provides for compensation of the party aggrieved by the breach of the contract. "The principle of award of compensation is that the injured party should as far as possible be placed in the same position in terms of money as if the contract had been performed by the party in default" (Pollock and Mulla in Indian Contract Act, 11th Edition P.801). Illustration (a) to the section supports this proposition of law. In case of a building contract for breach by the employer, the builder will be entitled to be placed in the same position as he would have been in had the contract been allowed to be performed. In performing the contract, the builder would have to spend money on materials, bear the labour cost and miscellaneous costs, if there be any, and the rest of the money agreed to be paid would be the profit of the builder. If the contract work could not be proceeded with, the builder would be entitled to get the expected profit as damages. If the contract is rescinded illegally by the employer in the midway, the builder would be entitled to the percentage of profit in respect of the unexecuted work. Certainly, the builder cannot claim the entire contract value which does not represent his expected profit. Where the department terminated the contract illegally, it was held that the builder was entitled to claim damages at the rate of 10% of the unexecuted amount of work which he could expect to earn by way of profit (Dwarka Das vs. State of MP, (1993)3 SCC 500). In AT Brij Paul Singh and Brothers vs State of Gujarat, AIR 1984 (SC) 703, the Indian Supreme Court held that 15% of the value of the balance of the-contract works was not an unreasonable measure of damages for the loss of profit. In the instant case, it is apparent on the face of the award that the Arbitrator proceeded totally ignoring the principle under lying the provision of section 73 of the Contract Act in passing an award of taka more than 7 (seven) crore in favour of the contractor when the total value of the contract was only Taka 99,49,729. The modification by the High Court Division also does not take into account the provision of section 73 of the Contract Act. The illegality of the award as well as the modification of it by the High Court Division, can be seen on a bare look at the award and its modification. The award is per se preposterous or absurd for which also the award and its modification are liable to be set-aside. In support of such finding, reliance may be placed on Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board vs Unique Erector (Gujarat) (P) Ltd. AIR 1989 (SC)1973. 

 19. In the instant case, the Arbitrator's defiance of the obvious policy enshrined in the provision of section 73 of the Contract Act is so blatant that the Court may be justified in coming to the conclusion that the Arbitrator was biased which became known only when the award was passed. 

 21. On the facts and in the circumstances of the case, we are inclined to hold that the respondent is entitled to Taka 15,00,000 on account of loss or damages caused by breach of contract and Taka 15,00,000 for purchasing construction materials and for defraying other costs totaling Taka 30,00,000 of which Taka 6,94,589 would be running bill taken by the respondent.
